deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a page of derivations. It is a run of dated, discovery-style entries in Gauss's hand from the summer of 1797 in Göttingen. Their content, wording and dates coincide with Gauss's scientific diary (Tagebuch), entries c. 63–70, published by Klein in 1903 and in Werke X.1. I am identifying this from the text, not from bundle documentation.

(1) Jun 17. 'Demonstrationes elegantiores pro nexu divisorum formae □−a, +1 cum −1, ±2 inveni.'
- 'Divisors of the form □−a' means primes p dividing x^2−a, i.e. primes for which a is a quadratic residue.
- The connection with −1 and ±2 is the first and second supplementary laws of quadratic reciprocity:
  - (−1/p) = (−1)^((p−1)/2);
  - (2/p) = (−1)^((p^2−1)/8);
  - (−2/p) = 1 iff p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8).
- Gauss records more elegant proofs. These were already proved by induction in 1796; compare Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (DA) arts. 108–116.

(2) Jul 17. 'Deductionem secundam theoriae polygonorum excolui.' He worked out a second derivation of the theory of the cyclotomic equation x^n−1=0, the polygon theory of DA Sect. VII.

(3) 'Per utramque methodum monstrari posse puras tantum aequationes solvi oportere.' By either method one shows that only pure equations y^k = A need to be solved. In modern terms, the period equations of x^n=1 reduce to binomial equations: cyclotomic equations are solvable by radicals (DA art. 359–360).

(4) Jul 20. 'Quod Oct. 1. per ind. invenimus demonstratione munivimus.' A result found by induction on 1 Oct 1796 has now been proved. Which result is not determinable from this page alone; see the diary entry of 1 Oct 1796.

(5) Jul 2? (the image most likely reads Jul. 21). The singular case of solving x^n − 1 ≡ 0 (mod p^k), 'when the auxiliary congruence has equal roots', is overcome.
- This is the case p | n. Then x^n − 1 has repeated roots mod p, the derivative n·x^(n−1) ≡ 0 mod p, and the naive (Newton/Hensel) lifting fails.
- Gauss reports success 'from the solution of congruences when the modulus is a power of a prime'.
- Modern content: the structure of the n-th roots of unity modulo p^k, including the case p | n. This connects to DA arts. 82–89, on primitive roots modulo prime powers.

(6) Begins Jul 23 and continues on the next page. Let A = x^(m+n) + a x^(m+n−1) + … be monic with integer coefficients. Suppose A is divided by a monic B = x^m + α x^(m−1) + … with rational coefficients, leaving no remainder (exact division is implicit; this is my reading).
- Then all coefficients of B are integers.
- The struck-out first wording reads: no α, β, … can be a proper fraction if all are rational.
- This is Gauss's lemma, published as DA art. 42: a monic factor in Q[x] of a monic polynomial in Z[x] lies in Z[x].
- Implicit modern proof (mine): Q[x] = Z[x] ∩ … by content multiplicativity. If A = B·C with B, C monic in Q[x], clear denominators to get dB·eC = de·A. Primitivity of products then forces d = e = 1.
errors: No mathematical errors visible; entries are statements without derivations.

In entry (6) the hypothesis that the division is exact (remainder zero) and that B, and the quotient, are monic with rational coefficients is completed only on the next page; on this page alone the statement is incomplete.

results.what: More elegant proofs of the relation between prime divisors of x^2−a and the characters of −1, 2, −2 (supplementary laws of quadratic reciprocity)
results.modern_name: First and second supplementary laws of quadratic reciprocity

results.what: Second derivation of cyclotomy (polygon theory); reduction to pure equations
results.modern_name: Gaussian periods; solvability of cyclotomic equations by radicals

results.what: Solution of x^n ≡ 1 (mod p^k) in the singular case p | n
results.modern_name: Roots of unity modulo prime powers; Hensel lifting in the degenerate (repeated root) case; structure of (Z/p^k)^*

results.what: A monic integer polynomial divisible by a monic rational polynomial forces the divisor to be integral

deep.surprise_reason: These are entries of Gauss's published mathematical diary (Klein 1903; Werke X.1), and all results appeared in the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae; nothing here is unknown or misattributed.

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(p-1, p) == (1 if p % 4 == 1 else -1) for p in primerange(3, 2000))
checkable.asserts: First supplementary law: (−1/p) = 1 iff p ≡ 1 mod 4

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(2, p) == (1 if p % 8 in (1, 7) else -1) for p in primerange(3, 2000))
checkable.asserts: Second supplementary law: (2/p) = 1 iff p ≡ ±1 mod 8

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(p-2, p) == (1 if p % 8 in (1, 3) else -1) for p in primerange(3, 2000))
[x for x in range(9) if pow(x, 3, 9) == 1] == [1, 4, 7]
checkable.asserts: Singular case p | n: x^3 ≡ 1 (mod 9) has exactly the 3 solutions 1, 4, 7, although the roots mod 3 collapse to x ≡ 1

checkable.sympy: all(len([x for x in range(p**2) if pow(x, p, p**2) == 1]) == p for p in [3, 5, 7, 11])
checkable.asserts: x^p ≡ 1 (mod p^2) has exactly p solutions (x ≡ 1 mod p) despite the repeated root mod p
Example of Gauss's lemma: x^4+4 = (x^2−2x+2)(x^2+2x+2), and the monic rational factors are integral
